newsitem.title: USA: Gulf of Mexico boom revives drilling indusry.
newsitem.headline: Gulf of Mexico boom revives drilling indusry.

text.p: A drilling boom in the Gulf of Mexico has brought new life to the once-moribund U.S. offshore oil service industry, with drilling rigs suddenly commanding steep premiums and company earnings on the rise.
Analysts, normally loathe to look too far down the road at the battered oil service industry, are going so far as to predict a long period of prosperity.

"Earnings growth for drilling companies should continue for several years as day rates rise toward levels necessary to justify replacement of the aging (offshore rig) fleet," Salomon Brothers said in a recent report.
Out of 38 oil service companies reporting results for the quarter ending June 30, 32 met or exceeded Salomon's earnings expectations, the report said.

According to Offshore Data Services, which tracks the offshore oil industry, rig utilization rates in the Gulf of Mexico are hovering around 90 percent, a level not seen since the early 1980s, when oil prices peaked near $40 a barrel.

After the 1970s oil boom went bust, dropping prices to $10 a barrel in 1986, the offshore industry was in shambles. Many companies shut down or merged and many rigs were scrapped. Worldwide, the rig fleet fell from 809 in 1985 to the current 629, according to Salomon Brothers.
In the Gulf of Mexico, 188 rigs were still under contract in 1985, but a year later the number fell to 91. Utilization rates hit bottom, at 24 percent, in August 1986.

Currently, some 162 rigs are working in the Gulf, the same number as in March 1982, said Offshore Data Services drilling editor Tom Marsh. "We've reached a point where, effectively, there are no rigs available," he said.

Day rates for drilling rigs, a key barometer of the industry's health, are rising along with demand. Rates for 300-foot jackup rigs, an industry staple, range from $31,000 to $45,000 a day, up from $25,000 a year ago, Marsh said.
"There was a time a few years ago when these rigs couldn't even find a job. They'd be working for $15,000 a day and some of the smaller rigs were working for as little as $7,000 a day," he said.
High-end semi-submersible rigs, used in deep water exploration and production, are bringing $110,000 to $125,000 a day, well above last year's rates of $64,000 to $90,000, Marsh said.
The Gulf's re-emergence is the result of several factors, including higher oil and gas prices and improved technology.
While energy prices have not soared as they did in the 1970s, they are "high enough to stimulate drilling, yet low enough to stimulate consumption," said Global Marine Inc. Chairman C. Russell Luigs.

Steadily growing demand, particularly in the world's developing countries, has kept a floor under oil prices and given the industry enough confidence in price stability to invest in long-term projects such as deepwater fields.

At the same time, technological improvements such as horizontal drilling and three-dimensional seismic surveys, which give geologists a better look at what lies beneath the earth's surface before drilling, have lowered the industry's costs of exploration and production.

"(Three-dimensional) seismic has a better success rate, which is what it boils down to. Also, more efficient drilling cuts time and cost -- and time is money when you have these kind of (rig) day rates," said Marsh.
While drilling is up all over the Gulf, the deepwater projects far off the coast are the greatest source of excitement. Billions of barrels of oil lie thousands of feet below the water's surface.

"They are talking about the deepwater Gulf containing as much oil as Alaska when it was first discovered. It's a very large oil province, but we're just starting to scratch the surface," said Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Vice President Arvind Sanger.
Most of the oil giants, led by Shell Oil, are either developing or planning deepwater fields in the Gulf. The fields are costly, but offer the promise of big payoffs.

Shell, a unit of Royal Dutch Petroleum and partner British Petroleum Co. Plc will spend $1.2 billion on their Mars field southeast of New Orleans. They expect to be producing 100,000 barrels of oil and 110 million cubic feet of gas a day from the area by early 1997.
According to the International Energy Agency in Paris, Gulf of Mexico oil production is expected to hit 2.1 million barrels a day by 2000, up from just over 1 million last year.

Just as the oil industry is turning to the Gulf, analysts are becoming big fans of the offshore companies. In an Aug. 9 report, Salomon Brothers rated seven out of 10 offshore drilling firms a buy. The other three were rated as "hold."
Sanger said his current offshore service favorites include Diamond Offshore Drilling Inc., Tidewater Inc. and Falcon Drilling Co. Inc..
Diamond Offshore is particularly strong in the deepwater drilling area, while Tidewater holds 35 percent of the world oil boat fleet and 45 percent in the Gulf.
Falcon, whose major investors include George Soros, has a big piece of the barge drilling market, which operates in shallow water, and has been buying jackups and deepwater assets.
Like all oil booms, however, this one could fizzle if production outstrips demand and causes prices to tumble.
Merrill Lynch, in a report last December, said that the additional gas supplies from the Gulf, in conjunction with others, may create concerns of a new U.S. supply bubble late in 1997.
But it said that oil from the Gulf's deepwater fields was expected only to slow the long U.S. production decline, not "radically alter supply/demand fundamentals."
There is also the possibility that offshore drillers, eying ever-bigger payoffs, could begin to build new rigs, which would increase the supply and take the upward pressure off rising dayrates.

That happened in the 1970s boom, but Offshore Data Services' Marsh said it was unlikely that history would repeat itself. Twenty years ago, experts were predicting oil prices of $100 a barrel and banks, eager to cash in, "were falling all over themselves to finance these things," he said.
Now, oil price projections are much more subdued. And banks, having seen what happened to the drilling industry in the 1980s, are being much more conservative with their money.
"It's not that easy to finance a rig anymore. You have to have a big contract in hand before the banks will even think about it," Marsh said.
